h1: Prefab Container Homes: Six Repeatable Module Sizes
seoTitle: Prefab Container Homes | 6 Sizes & Prices | SAMAN Portable
metaDescription: Prefab container homes in six module sizes, 160 to 480 sq.ft, from Rs 2,86,000 ex-GST. Built to a repeating BOM for single homes and multi-unit colonies.
opener: A prefab container home is a factory-built residential module produced to a repeating bill of materials, so the twentieth unit leaves the line the same as the first. The buyers on this page are families building one home and estate owners, developers and site managers ordering five to twenty units as a single colony. What separates this page from the rest of the container house range is repeatability: a controlled floor cassette, a fixed panel batch, a standard wet pod, and an end wall kept blank so modules couple. Six sizes run from 20 x 8 ft at 160 sq.ft to 40 x 12 ft at 480 sq.ft, priced from Rs 2,86,000 ex-GST against a 200 sq.ft base rate of Rs 1,625 per sq.ft. Every size is 8 ft 6 in external and 8 ft internal, with 50 mm class insulated panels.

applicationsContent.h2: Six prefab module sizes, drawn to the same standard
applicationsContent.intro: Each size below has its own 3D general arrangement drawing, with dimensions, the opening schedule and the coupling interface on one sheet.

panels.h3: 20 x 8 ft prefab module: the 160 sq.ft colony unit
panels.paragraph: The 160 sq.ft module is the smallest unit SAMAN still calls a home rather than a cabin, and the one that repeats most often. Internal clear is 19 ft 6 in by 7 ft 6 in under an 8 ft ceiling, planned as a single 1 BHK run: living at the entry, a kitchen and dining band, a bedroom, and the wet pod on the corridor wall. End wall D stays blank so the unit couples. At 8 ft wide it moves on a standard trailer profile, which is why staff housing and site colonies order it in tens.
applications: 160 sq.ft built-up, 19 ft 6 in x 7 ft 6 in internal clear, 8 ft ceiling
Rs 2,86,000 ex-GST, Rs 3,37,480 including 18 per cent GST
Rs 1,787.50 per sq.ft, the 200 sq.ft base plus the 10 per cent band premium
3 windows and the entry door on wall A, 2 windows on wall B
Three units coupled give a 60 ft run at 480 sq.ft on one utility corridor
Narrowest of the six, so the least restricted road move

panels.h3: 20 x 10 ft prefab module: the standard 1 BHK layout

Two feet of extra width over the 20 x 8 change the plan rather than the length, so living takes a seating layout instead of a corridor and the kitchen gets a working counter run. Internal clear is 19 ft 6 in by 9 ft 6 in. It is the size most single-home buyers settle on.

panels.h3: 20 x 12 ft prefab module: width for the family plan

Where the plot depth is narrow it is the largest module that still parks inside a 20 ft bay, and in a colony it is the unit used where a family takes one module instead of two coupled ones.

descriptionHtml:
Is a prefab container home the same as a container house?

The two words do different work. A container house is the product category: a steel-framed, panel-clad dwelling built on a container-derived chassis, in whatever size and layout a site needs. Prefab describes how it is made. A prefab container home is one that has been standardised for repeat production, which means the drawing, the bill of materials, the panel batch and the pack list are fixed before the first unit is cut, and stay fixed for every unit after it.

That distinction matters because it changes what you are buying. If you want one house and you want it shaped around your plot, your view and your budget, you are shopping the container house range, and the size and bedroom decision is the one to make first. If you want five, ten or twenty dwellings that behave identically, or one house whose spare parts will still be available in three years, you are shopping this page. The two overlap in materials and finish; they diverge completely in how much of the build is decided in advance.

Buyers searching for prefab homes, prefabricated houses or modular housing in India usually land somewhere between the two, and the honest answer is that SAMAN builds both. What follows is written for the prefab decision specifically: what is standardised, what is still yours to choose, and what it costs at each of the six sizes.

What SAMAN fixes in the factory, and why it matters

Five things are fixed in the factory, and they are the reason the units match. The floor cassette is built on a production jig rather than measured on the shop floor, so every module in a batch is dimensionally interchangeable. The wall panels are cut from one approved batch, so colour, metal thickness, core and joint profile do not drift between unit three and unit fourteen. The roof cassette is trial-fitted in the factory before dispatch, so the site sequence is known rather than discovered. The wet pod is a standard assembly, tested before it leaves, with hot, cold, waste and vent stubs landing in the same position on every unit. And end wall D is kept clear of glazing, so any two modules can be coupled through it.

What that buys on site is a different kind of work. Panels arrive cut, labelled and sequenced against an erection drawing and a pack list. The joints are dry: bolted plates at the corner posts, a closure profile and flashing at the seam, and sealant used to weather a properly supported lap rather than to make up for one. There is no wet trade waiting on another wet trade, which is why a colony run compresses so much faster than a conventional build.

It also changes what happens when something goes wrong. Because the standard is written down, a deviation gets recorded against a unit number instead of absorbed silently. If unit nine needed a heavier floor for a particular load, that is on the schedule, and unit ten is still the standard. Three years later, a replacement wall panel or floor sheet is ordered against the same batch reference and still fits the opening.

None of this is a claim about performance. Thermal, fire and acoustic behaviour depend on the exact panel supplied and the evidence that came with it, not on the words PUF or mineral wool. SAMAN states the panel that was supplied and the report that supports it; where there is no report, there is no rating.

How the six sizes behave when you repeat them

The six sizes are not six products. They are one module drawn at six footprints, which is why they share an 8 ft 6 in external height, an 8 ft internal ceiling, a 3 in wall, roof and floor build-up, a 4 ft by 3 ft window module and a 3 ft by 7 ft entry door. What changes between them is area, the planning template and the opening count.

The three 20 ft sizes carry a 1 BHK template: living at the entry, a kitchen and dining band, one bedroom, and the wet pod on the corridor wall. Width is what separates them. At 8 ft the living zone is circulation with furniture in it; at 10 ft it takes a seating layout; at 12 ft dining separates from living and a fourth window is added. The three 40 ft sizes carry the compact 2 BHK template, with the second bedroom at the far end and the wet pod between the two. Again width decides quality rather than count: 8 ft gives two bedrooms in a corridor plan, 10 ft gives both of them usable depth, 12 ft separates the dining zone.

When they are repeated, width also decides the site plan. Modules couple end to end through wall D, so three 20 ft units make a 60 ft run and three 40 ft units make a 120 ft run, each on a single external utility corridor. A colony of mixed sizes still works because the corridor position and the stub layout are constant; what varies is how many bays each unit occupies. That is the practical reason SAMAN keeps the wet core on one wall across all six sizes rather than optimising each plan separately.

Road movement is the other constraint that scales. The 8 ft wide modules move on a standard trailer profile. The 10 ft and 12 ft modules are over-width, so transport, escorts and route survey are quoted per project rather than assumed. On a twenty-unit order that difference is often larger than the difference in unit price, and it is worth settling before the size is frozen.

Costing a colony against costing one house

A single house and a colony are priced from the same rate card but they are not the same commercial exercise. SAMAN's rate is set at the 200 sq.ft reference: Rs 1,625 per sq.ft. Below 200 sq.ft the rate goes up, because the fixed content of a module does not shrink with area. Above 200 sq.ft it comes down band by band, to a floor at 900 sq.ft beyond which a project quotation replaces the ladder.

The table below is the ladder as it applies to the six prefab sizes, and it is the same arithmetic the price shown on this page uses.

On a colony, three things move that the table does not show. The first is the prototype: bulk production only starts after one sample unit is approved and the site connection coordinates are frozen, and that approval cycle is real time on the programme. The second is aggregation: electrical and water loads for the whole run are worked out at site level, not by multiplying one unit, and the result can require infrastructure that no individual unit price includes. The third is sequencing: units delivered in batches against an erection programme cost less to install than the same units delivered at once and stored.

The honest way to read the ladder, then, is as the module price. It tells you what a unit costs ex-works against approved drawings. Everything that makes a group of units into a colony sits outside it and is quoted against the site.

What the price covers and what stays outside it

What the module price covers is the repeatable factory-built residential module: the structural base and frame, the 50 mm class insulated panel envelope, the roof cassette, the standard interior finish, the internal partitions and ceiling, electrical wiring to the approved layout, and the compact wet-service provision. What it does not cover is everything that depends on your site, and that list is worth reading before you compare quotations.

  • Foundations, plinths, levelling and any site civil work
  • Transport, unloading, craneage and installation beyond the agreed scope
  • Colony infrastructure: roads, drainage, external water, sewage treatment and site power
  • Utility connections from the corridor stubs to the site network, and final testing
  • Furniture, appliances, air conditioning equipment and loose fittings
  • Premium finish, kitchen and sanitary upgrades above the standard schedule
  • Statutory approvals, permissions and project-specific engineering or testing

Two of those deserve a note. Interior fit-out beyond the standard finish is quoted separately rather than bundled, because a premium kitchen or sanitary schedule on a twenty-unit order is a different negotiation from the same upgrade on one house. And transport and installation are excluded from the ladder rather than estimated into it, because the difference between an 8 ft wide module on a standard trailer and a 12 ft module needing an over-width move is too large to average.

Getting a site ready before the modules arrive

Modules arrive finished, which means the site has to be finished first. The base has to be level, squared and able to take the module's support points where the general arrangement drawing shows them, not wherever the crane happens to reach. Bearing, anchor positions, corrosion access and the full load path are on the signed GA and the structural drawings; a nominal channel section quoted on a web page is not a substitute for a foundation design or a site wind review.

Access matters as much as the base. A 40 ft module needs a turning radius and a hardstanding for the vehicle and the lifting equipment, and it needs them in the same week the module is on the road. On colony work the erection sequence usually dictates the access route rather than the other way round, which is why the pack list and the erection drawing are issued together.

Services are the third item. External networks, tanks, pumps, sewage treatment and final testing sit outside the module scope, and the module simply presents labelled stubs at the utility corridor. Getting those networks to the corridor line before the modules land is what separates a two-day installation from a two-week one. SAMAN publishes a 7 to 21 working day lead time on the module itself; the site programme is yours.

Warranty, service life and what falls outside cover

SAMAN gives a 10-year structural warranty on the steel structure of its container homes, and a 1-year finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on the finish package. The exact period, start date, remedy, service access and relocation conditions are the ones written into the signed quotation and the handover documents; the figures here describe the standard offer, not a substitute for those documents.

What falls outside cover is consistent across the range and worth stating plainly: unapproved alterations, poor or settling foundations, water entering the building at the site interface, utility faults, corrosive exposure the module was not specified for, missed seal and coating maintenance, misuse, and damage caused by relocating a module. Relocation in particular is a common misunderstanding on prefab work. A module is designed to be transported once to its site and installed; repeated relocation is a different specification and a different conversation.

Service life follows maintenance more than it follows the specification. The items that decide it are the coating system at cut edges and penetrations, the sealant and closure profiles at panel joints and module seams, and the roof drainage. All three are accessible by design on a SAMAN module, which is deliberate: a joint you cannot inspect is a joint you cannot maintain.

Where prefab sits against the rest of the range

Inside the container house range, each page answers a different question, and it is worth knowing which one you are actually asking. The range page answers how big and how many bedrooms. This page answers whether the unit needs to repeat. Shipping container homes answer what happens when the build has to be relocatable or coastal, and the specification changes to reinforced corner posts, a heavier shell and coastal sealing. Luxury container houses answer finish level at the same footprint.

Three more decisions sit outside this page. If the constraint is transport rather than production, flat-pack construction ships the module as panels and assembles it at site. If the constraint is footprint after placement, an expandable unit opens out once it is landed. And if the requirement is workforce accommodation at scale rather than housing, that is a labour colony brief, with different densities, sanitation ratios and compliance obligations, and it belongs on its own page.

SAMAN manufactures in its own works at Greater Noida in the north zone and Bengaluru in the south, and is an ISO 9001:2015 certified manufacturer with more than 500 completed projects delivered. Delivery is pan-India, free inside Bengaluru city and across Delhi NCR. If your requirement is a single home, the fastest route is to pick a size above and ask for the drawing. If it is a colony, send the unit count and the site, and the quotation will come back with the module price and the site scope separated, which is the only way the two numbers can be checked.

FAQs

What is the difference between a prefab container home and a container house?

A container house is the product; prefab describes how it is made. A prefab container home is standardised for repeat production, so the drawing, bill of materials, panel batch and pack list are fixed before the first unit is cut.

What does a prefab container home cost in India?

SAMAN's six prefab module sizes run from Rs 2,86,000 ex-GST at 160 sq.ft to Rs 7,33,200 ex-GST at 480 sq.ft, against a 200 sq.ft base rate of Rs 1,625 per sq.ft adjusted by area band. Add 18 per cent GST.

How many prefab modules can be joined together?

Modules couple end to end through end wall D, which is kept clear of glazing for that purpose. Three 20 ft units make a 60 ft run and three 40 ft units a 120 ft run, each served by one external utility corridor.

How long does a prefab container home take to build?

SAMAN publishes a 7 to 21 working day lead time on the module itself. On colony orders, bulk production starts only after one prototype unit is approved and the site connection coordinates are frozen.

Is transport and installation included in the price?

No. The price shown is the module price ex-works against approved drawings. Transport, unloading, craneage, installation beyond the agreed scope, foundations and site utilities are quoted separately against the site.

What warranty comes with a prefab container home?

A 10-year structural warranty on the steel structure and a 1-year finishing warranty extendable to 2 years. The period, remedy and exclusions written into the signed quotation and handover documents govern.

Can a prefab container home be moved after installation?

It is designed to be transported once to its site and installed. Repeated relocation is a different specification, and damage caused by relocating a module falls outside the standard warranty.
